title: Whether Indians and liquor mix badly
summary: He argues that holding liquor depends on the person, not on race, though Indians had reason to feel desperate given their situation.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But is that true in your experience that Indians didn't take liquor very well? I mean, do you think they got disorderly quicker than others?
Well, I'll tell you what I really think. I've seen a lot of Indians that drink and that could drink and I've seen Indians that couldn't drink.

I've seen Indians that could drink and Indians that couldn't drink. You see, because I think it's the person. Having been around so many of them, you know what I mean. But I think it's really the person because I've seen friends of mine that could drink and friends that couldn't drink and if they got so much in them, they just went the other way, you know? So consequently, then, too, I think Indians felt -- it wasn't hard for them to go haywire. I think due to the way the situation and everything was and had been, you know.
And when a guy's got things on his mind like that, it creates a different story, complete different atmosphere.

That's right. And -- because I have seen some that take it. I mean, they sit there and drink and never change, you know what I mean. But they often seem to think -- you know, you read a lot about -- they say, "Well, when he'd get that firewater in him, he would go crazy," you know. But he didn't go crazier than anybody else, you know, that couldn't handle it. He didn't go any crazier. You know, that's the way I see it.

But that's the truth. It's the same with any people. I mean, some people really haven't got the stomach for liquor. Some people don't eat right. And then some people makes them mean and evil and other people, it makes them jolly and foolish.
